newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-French markets weak on talk of EU pact delay.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-French markets weak on talk of EU pact delay.

text.p: French markets were shaken on Monday as investors reacted to the Socialist-led government's calls for a "period of reflection" on a pact limiting budget deficits of countries that join a common European currency.
Analysts said the French demand, which amounted to a delay in the timetable for ratification of the so-called stability pact, added uncertainty to the creation of the euro.

While few questioned France's commitment to starting European economic and monetary union (EMU) on time, the main concern among analysts was that the French position could cause a rift with Germany and throw the whole project into doubt.

"France clearly wants EMU with the stability pact delayed or renegotiated but the question is whether the Germans will use this as a pretext to seek a delay in monetary union," Philippe Brossard, head of research at ABN Amro Finance, said.
The Paris Bourse, which was trading lower before the comments, slid to 2.2 percent down before bouncing off the bottom to stabilise at 2,686.20, off 1.2 percent.

The franc fell by more than half a centime to 3.3825 per mark but held above last week's low of 3.3860 set after the left swept to power in a June 1 election upset. At 1500 GMT it was at 3.3790 per mark.

"The risk is more that the market sees a real conflict between France and Germany - some of the comments coming out from (German finance minister Theo) Waigel sound unfriendly - even though in the longer run it does not mean an end to EMU if there's no stability pact in Amsterdam," said Sonja Gibbs, bond analyst at Nomura International.

The new French government, headed by Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, set down several conditions during the election for going ahead with EMU, including the participation of Italy and the creation of an economic government to offset the power of a future independent European central bank.

However, he said the conditions, along with his reservations about the stability pact, should serve as a basis for discussion and that France was still committed to launching the single currency on time.

"It would appear from this that the Socialist government is maybe a little more serious ultimately than some had taken them to be. Jospin wants to maintain his credibility," said Iain Lindsay, senior bond analyst at Credit Lyonnais.

French bond futures fell heavily from their earlier highs but clung to positive ground. The yield spread between German and French 10 year bonds, a gauge of investor risk assessment, narrowed to minus six basis points from minus nine on Friday.
"I don't think people are so much buying Germany. (German bonds) are outperforming as they're not being sold as much as France," Gibbs said.
June PIBOR futures, which were slightly positive before the comments, also fell, ending the day down three basis points, also off their lows.

French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn called on Monday for a period of reflection before agreeing to the stability pact. He said France was not seeking to renegotiate the pact and was totally committed to a timely EMU start.

Diplomats said Strauss-Kahn told European Union ministers in Luxembourg that Jospin wanted to inform the National Assembly about the pact on June 19, two days after an EU summit was supposed to have approved the agreement in Amsterdam.
The new French cabinet was planning a special meeting this Thursday to discuss policy priorities and Jospin is expected to present his programme on June 19.

Economists said the added uncertainty could cause volatility in French markets until it was clear a compromise could be reached on the pact, which Bonn sees as crucial to maintaining a credible euro currency.
"Until they kiss and make up, we could see the franc go up and down," said Steven Englander, economist at Smith Barney.
